Northwind's invoices exported with the wrong tax rate for their Dutch entity, and their finance team only caught it after some had already been sent to their own clients — they emailed Marco about it on Sunday night [[M2#16]]. The cause was a rounding change made in August, which only affected accounts with multiple tax jurisdictions — essentially just Northwind [[M2#17]]. Forty-one invoices over two weeks were affected; Diego could fix the calculation the same day, but regenerating the already-sent PDFs was the awkward part [[M2#19]].

Resolution:
- Diego fixed the calculation that day and sent Northwind a list of the affected invoice numbers by the next morning so they could issue corrections; Marco called their CFO himself [[M2#20]][[M2#21]].
- No compensation was promised in the note — Marco held that decision until after the call [[M2#23]].
- By the September 15 sync the issue was closed: corrected invoices had gone out, Northwind's finance team confirmed the numbers, and the CFO replied [[M3#9]]. Marco then gave them one month free, with Ana applying the credit that day [[M3#10]][[M3#11]].

No. The mobile app was cut from Q4 and the decision has held all month.

- Sept 1: Marco decided "no mobile app in Q4," to be revisited in January if the mobile share changes [[M1#25]]. The reasoning: only ~8% of sessions are on a phone, mostly people checking invoice status, which the responsive site already handles [[M1#23]], and it would consume the whole quarter for two people [[M1#24]]. Sofía added a note to the support macro so the team stops promising it [[M1#26]].
- Sept 8: Marco restated it — Q4 is pricing, then checkout, then SOC 2 groundwork, nothing added unless something is removed; "the mobile app is not happening… January at the earliest" [[M2#25]]. He posted that in writing in the channel for Sofía to link from the support macro [[M2#26]][[M2#27]].
- Sept 29 retro: Marco said the mobile app was cut on purpose with "zero regrets," since the people asking want a feature the responsive site already has [[M5#23]].

One caution: an AI note-taker summary claimed the team had decided to build the mobile app — Sofía flagged it as the opposite of the actual decision, and the trial was cancelled for that reason [[M3#19]][[M3#23]].

**Drata**, decided at the September 29 retro [[M5#19]].

Why: Marco brought three quotes — Vanta, Drata, and Secureframe — all within twenty percent of each other on price, so price wasn't the deciding factor. Drata had the best Postgres and GitHub integrations, which cover most of the team's evidence collection; Vanta's advantage was only a nicer dashboard, and Secureframe was cheapest but had a smaller auditor network [[M5#16]]. Diego, who has to feed the platform, said integrations matter more than the dashboard [[M5#17]], and Sofía agreed on Drata [[M5#18]].

Note the shortlist widened along the way: in Q4 planning on September 1 the evaluation was limited to Vanta and Drata [[M1#21]][[M1#22]], but Secureframe was added by the retro [[M5#16]].

Next steps: Marco signs in the first week of October, Diego kicks off the integrations after the checkout change ships, so late October [[M5#19]]. The audit itself is Q1, since evidence collection takes three months minimum, and Marco will tell Northwind that timeline [[M5#22]].

The biggest drop-off is at the **billing address step** in checkout.

- Originally the team only knew they lost "about a third of people between picking a plan and confirming payment," without knowing which step, because the funnel events weren't granular enough [[M1#10]]. Diego guessed the address form, since a full billing address is requested even for card payments and Stripe doesn't need it [[M1#11]].
- After Diego shipped the funnel instrumentation [[M2#10]], the first week of data showed the billing address screen as the biggest drop: **28% of people who pick a plan leave on that screen** [[M2#11]].
- With two more weeks of data, the figure settled at **29% at the billing address step**, flat across plans and countries [[M3#1]]. That's the latest number.

Consequence: remove the address step for card payments (Stripe validates the postcode itself), keeping it for bank transfer and invoice-based plans; Diego and Ana build it, shipping one week after the pricing page, around 22 October [[M3#1]][[M3#6]][[M3#7]].

**Sep 15 (weekly sync)**

**Sep 22 (design review with Priya)**

- Annual discount cut from twenty percent to **fifteen**, at finance's request; Marco owned the decision [[M4#6]][[M4#11]].
- Show the saving both ways: percent on the toggle, currency amount under each price [[M4#9]][[M4#10]][[M4#11]].
- Comparison table stays below the fold, with anchor links from each tier to its column [[M4#16]][[M4#17]].
- **No fourth enterprise tier** — just one line under the table, "Need more than fifty seats? Talk to us.", since only two accounts are enterprise and a fourth tier shrinks the other three [[M4#20]][[M4#21]][[M4#22]].
- Free tier shows "0 dollars" in the same position as the other prices, so the number rhythm holds [[M4#24]][[M4#25]].
- Launch still on for the fifteenth, with legal copy due the next day [[M4#26]][[M4#27]].

On September 1, Sofía flagged that about a third of users drop between picking a plan and confirming payment but said she couldn't say which step because funnel events weren't granular enough [[M1#10]]. Two items were explicitly left unowned, plus one that stayed with an outside party:

**1. Checkout abandonment analysis — raised unowned on Sept 1, owned by Sofía on Sept 8.**
Marco asked "who owns this?" [[M1#13]]; Sofía said someone should look at it properly with instrumentation but she had no bandwidth that month because of the pricing analysis [[M1#14]], and Diego offered only to add the funnel events, not the analysis [[M1#15]]. Marco left it "on the list without an owner for now" to revisit the next week [[M1#16]]. On Sept 8, once Diego's events shipped [[M2#10]] and the data showed a 28% drop at the billing address step [[M2#11]], Sofía volunteered to own it [[M2#13]] and Marco confirmed: "Sofía owns checkout abandonment" [[M2#14]]. She then took the follow-up proposal, due the next Monday [[M2#15]], and delivered it on Sept 15 [[M3#1]]; the resulting build went to Diego and Ana [[M3#6]].

**2. The refund wording / rewritten refund copy — never owned internally; it sat with legal throughout.**
On Sept 1 the copy was the open piece, waiting on Carla from legal to sign off on the refund wording — no internal owner [[M1#3]]. On Sept 8 it escalated: legal wanted the section rewritten, Carla wanted a lawyer to draft it, and the lawyer's earliest slot was the 23rd [[M2#1]] — still no one on the team owning it, which is what pushed the launch to October 15 [[M2#5]]. On Sept 15 Ana reported legal "on track for the twenty-third" [[M3#13]], and on Sept 22 she still described the copy as the one thing outstanding, "which legal sends tomorrow" [[M4#0]]. So it got a date but never a team owner — Marco's retro conclusion was to stop "planning around dates other people control" [[M5#23]].

**3. Related: an owned task that became unowned.** The SOC 2 vendor quotes were Marco's from the start [[M1#20]], and he still held them on Sept 15 with two of three in hand [[M3#15]]. At the retro he chose Drata and kept the contract signature [[M5#19]], but declared he would no longer own procurement tasks because he "sat on the quotes for a month" [[M5#23]] — no replacement owner was named in that meeting.

Sofía raised the mobile app at Q4 planning on September 1, but argued against building it: support keeps getting asked for it, yet only eight percent of sessions are on a phone, and most of those are people checking invoice status, which the responsive site already handles [[M1#23]] [[M1#22]]. After Marco decided against it for Q4 [[M1#25]], she offered to put a note in the support macro so the team stops promising it [[M1#26]].

On September 8, when Marco restated that the mobile app is not happening and January is the earliest [[M2#25]], Sofía asked him to put the roadmap statement in writing so she could link it from the support macro [[M2#26]].

As of the September 29 retro:

- **Vendor:** Drata, chosen over Vanta and Secureframe because it has the best Postgres and GitHub integrations, which cover most of the evidence [[M5#16]][[M5#19]]. Prices were all within twenty percent of each other; Diego backed integrations over Vanta's dashboard [[M5#16]][[M5#17]].
- **Contract:** Marco signs in the first week of October [[M5#19]].
- **Integrations kickoff:** Diego starts them after the checkout change ships, so late October [[M5#19]][[M5#20]].
- **Evidence collection:** three months minimum [[M5#22]].
- **Audit:** not this year — Q1 [[M5#22]]. Marco was to tell Northwind that timeline that week [[M5#22]].

Background: SOC 2 came up in Q4 planning because two customers asked for it in August, one being Northwind, the biggest account; the controls mostly exist, so the work is evidence collection and the audit, which needs a vendor platform [[M1#18]][[M1#19]]. Marco originally planned to bring two or three quotes to the end-of-month retro, initially scoped to Vanta and Drata [[M1#20]][[M1#21]][[M1#22]]; by September 15 he had two of three [[M3#15]]. SOC 2 is third in the Q4 order, after pricing and checkout [[M2#25]]. Marco acknowledged the start is late because he sat on the quotes for a month, and said he'll no longer own procurement tasks [[M5#23]].

At the September 22 design review, Marco asked whether the pricing page should have an enterprise "contact us" tier, a question he kept getting from sales [[M4#18]]. Priya first asked whether they actually sell enterprise; Marco said two accounts, one of them Northwind [[M4#19]][[M4#20]]. Her recommendation: not a tier, but a single line under the comparison table — "Need more than fifty seats? Talk to us." — because a fourth tier makes the three look smaller [[M4#21]]. Marco agreed: one line, no fourth tier [[M4#22]], and Ana took it on [[M4#23]].

Carla never speaks in any of these meetings — the participants are Ana, Diego, Marco, Sofía, and (in the design review) Priya. She's only referred to by others: Ana said Carla from legal still had to sign off on the refund wording for the pricing page copy [[M1#3]], and a week later that legal wanted the refund section rewritten rather than tweaked, with Carla wanting a lawyer to draft it, the earliest slot being the twenty-third [[M2#1]].

**Order: pricing page → checkout → SOC 2 groundwork**, in that sequence, and "nothing gets added unless something gets removed" [[M2#25]].

**Why it matters (Marco's reasoning):** each change moves the numbers the next one depends on. If checkout changes launch the same week as pricing, "we won't know which one moved conversion, and we'll spend November arguing about it instead of shipping" — so one thing at a time, measured, then the next [[M2#25]].

The principle was set from the start: Sofía argued at Q4 planning for launching pricing before the checkout work, otherwise she couldn't tell which change moved the numbers, and Marco agreed [[M1#6]][[M1#7]]. It has held through the schedule slip — when pricing moved to October 15, Marco explicitly chose not to overlap rather than run them in parallel [[M2#5]] — and drove the checkout decision: the billing-address removal gets built now but ships one week after pricing is live and has a week of data, around October 22 [[M3#5]][[M3#6]][[M3#7]].

The same sequencing pushes adjacent work behind it: Diego held the production Postgres upgrade until the week after pricing launches [[M2#8]], and the mobile app is excluded from Q4 entirely — January at the earliest [[M2#25]].
